newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Rebels say Pakistan helping Sri Lanka troops.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say Pakistan helping Sri Lanka troops.

text.p: Tamil Tiger rebels on Friday accused Pakistan of helping Sri Lanka's military plan the current offensive by government troops, now consolidating positions breached in a recent daring attack by the guerrillas.

"Sri Lanka's Operation Jaya Sikuru -- the military operation currently in progress -- was planned jointly with Pakistani military officials," a statement from Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) said.
The rebels said they received their information from reliable independent sources.
"There is no truth in this allegation," a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters at a news briefing in Islamabad. In Colombo, a Pakistani High Commission spokesman echoed the denial.
"We totally deny it. The conflict is an internal affair of Sri Lanka. Pakistan does not interfere in the internal matter of any country," the spokesman told Reuters.
Officials at Sri Lanka's foreign ministry were not immediately available for comment.

"Pakistani officials converged at Sri Lanka's (northern) Anuradhapura army headquarters immediately prior to the launch of the military offensive, which has now run into difficulties following Tuesday's LTTE strike at Thandikulam," the rebels' statement said.

About 20,000 troops launched Operation Jaya Sikuru through the brush jungles of the Wanni last month in an attempt to open a crucial highway linking the northern government-held Vavuniya town to Jaffna peninsula, 100 km (60 miles) further north.
The troops have captured key rebel towns in the area.

But more than 1,000 rebels mounted a daring raid earlier this week on the military's defence positions at Thandikulam and Nochchimodai, near the government-held town of Vavuniya which lies some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.

A Defence Ministry spokesman said on Friday that troops on a month-long thrust into Tamil Tiger rebel areas were consolidating their positions and patching up defences breached in this week's rebel assault.
"Our troops are consolidating their positions," a Defence Ministry spokesman said.
Analysts and diplomats have said the daring Tamil rebel counterattack, while costly for both sides, would not halt the military's offensive against the rebels.

Military officials said the army's death toll in the raid was expected to be around 140 but the LTTE, fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east, have said more than 300 soldiers were killed along with 50 guerrillas.
The Defence Ministry said rebel radio indicated 320 LTTE fighters had died in the assault. Earlier ministry estimates said 210 rebels died.

In a fresh attack in the east on Friday, rebels stopped a passenger bus and shot dead three policemen and two civilians at Onthachchimadam, near Kallar, in Batticaloa district 240 km (150 miles) east of Colombo.
The policemen were going home on leave.
Independent confirmation of developments has not been possible since international media have not been allowed into the war zone.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
